summary.text: The counterexample is the boundary case \(n=0\): the divisor sums and totient contribution give \(a(0)=0\), although \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime. Thus the formulation over all natural numbers fails because it includes \(0\), whereas the intended claim begins at \(n=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma(n)-2n^2,
\]
where
\[
\sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^2,
\qquad
\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d.
\]
The universally quantified assertion that is disproved extends this definition to every natural number, including \(0\), with the conventions that the finite divisor set of \(0\) is empty and that \(\varphi(0)=0\). (If the expression is regarded as an integer and then converted to a natural number by replacing negative values by zero, that conversion has no effect in the calculation below, since the expression is exactly zero.)

Take \(n=0\). By the stated divisor-set convention, there are no elements in the finite set over which either divisor sum is taken. Hence both empty sums are zero:
\[
\sigma_2(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d^2=0,
\qquad
\sigma(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d=0.
\]
Also \(\varphi(0)=0\). This follows directly from the interpretation of \(\varphi(n)\) as the number of natural numbers \(k<n\) that are coprime to \(n\): there is no natural number \(k<0\). Finally, \(0^2=0\). Therefore
\[
A(0)
 =\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma(0)-2\cdot 0^2
 =0+0\cdot 0-0
 =0.
\]
Thus the left-hand side of the proposed equivalence
\[
A(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\ \text{or}\ n\text{ is prime}
\]
is true when \(n=0\).

Its right-hand side is false at \(n=0\). Certainly \(0\ne1\). Moreover, \(0\) is not prime: a prime natural number is at least \(2\) (and, equivalently, has exactly the positive divisors \(1\) and itself), whereas \(0<2\). Consequently
\[
0=1\ \text{or}\ 0\text{ is prime}
\]
is false.

Hence, at \(n=0\), the equivalence asserting that \(A(n)=0\) exactly for \(n=1\) or prime \(n\) has a true left-hand side and a false right-hand side. It therefore fails. Since the full proposed statement requires this equivalence, together with the characterization of the value \(2\), to hold for every natural number, failure of the first equivalence at this one value is enough to refute the entire conjunction; no analysis of the value-\(2\) clause is needed.

Thus the assertion quantified over all natural numbers is false, with counterexample \(n=0\).

This counterexample depends essentially on including \(0\) in the quantified domain. The canonical OEIS conjecture is stated only for \(n\ge1\). Therefore \(n=0\) is not a counterexample to that restricted statement; the argument disproves only its extension to all natural numbers that includes zero.
